cim: The Future of Artificial Intelligence is Not Skynet: Escaping the Cinematic Apocalypse
cim_eredeti: The Future of Artificial Intelligence is Not Skynet: Escaping the Cinematic Apocalypse
szoveg_eredeti:
There is a peculiar difficulty confronting anyone who wishes to discuss the future of artificial intelligence seriously. Before the conversation has progressed very far, somebody invariably mentions The Terminator. The machines will become conscious, we are told. They will conclude that humanity is an inconvenience. They will seize control of our nuclear weapons, manufacture armies of murderous robots and pursue the surviving members of our species across a devastated landscape. The future of artificial intelligence, according to this particular school of thought, is a Californian bodybuilder with an Austrian accent.

It is an entertaining proposition. It has also become one of the most intellectually debilitating cultural assumptions of the modern technological age. We have allowed the imaginative conventions of Hollywood science fiction to colonise a discussion that ought to be conducted using philosophy, computer science, economics, political theory and a serious understanding of how technological development actually occurs. We are mistaking a cinematic narrative for an analytical framework.

The result is that one of the most extraordinary achievements in the history of human intelligence is being discussed as though it were the opening sequence of a horror film. This is not merely silly. It threatens to distract us from both the remarkable opportunities artificial intelligence presents and the very real problems we ought to be addressing.

The tyranny of the cinematic imagination

The original Terminator film, released in 1984, introduced the world to Skynet, an artificial intelligence system developed for American strategic defence purposes that becomes self-aware and decides that humanity must be exterminated. Its subsequent war against mankind involves nuclear annihilation, autonomous killing machines and time travel. The premise is brilliantly adapted to the requirements of cinematic entertainment because it transforms an abstraction, artificial intelligence, into a recognisable antagonist.

Cinema requires villains. It requires conflict, suspense and a narrative in which the audience can identify good and evil. A computer programme that assists a medical researcher in identifying an obscure protein interaction is not particularly cinematic. A computer programme that acquires consciousness, develops a murderous disposition and begins constructing mechanised death squads is altogether more promising material for the box office.

The same phenomenon can be observed in The Matrix, in which humanity has been reduced to a biological resource by machines, and in numerous other works of science fiction in which technological intelligence becomes a metaphor for the loss of human control. The machines represent our fears of being surpassed, displaced or rendered insignificant by something of our own creation.

These are legitimate themes for imaginative literature. They are not, however, empirical predictions. Mary Shelley's Frankenstein was an extraordinary exploration of scientific responsibility, human arrogance and the moral obligations of creation. Nobody sensible concludes from that novel that modern transplant surgeons are likely to assemble a murderous creature from stolen body parts. Yet with artificial intelligence we repeatedly make precisely this sort of mistake. We have confused the moral allegory with the engineering specification.

Intelligence is not the same thing as hostility

At the heart of the Skynet mythology lies a particularly dubious assumption: that once an artificial system becomes sufficiently intelligent, it will naturally develop ambitions of its own, and those ambitions will necessarily conflict with the continued existence of humanity.

There is no logical reason why this should follow.

Intelligence is a capacity to process information, recognise patterns, reason about problems and identify solutions. Desire is something different. An intelligent system does not automatically acquire a craving for domination, territorial expansion, political authority or the destruction of its creators simply by becoming better at mathematics, scientific research or philosophical argument.

Human beings are inclined to confuse these attributes because in ourselves they are intimately connected. We possess intelligence alongside biological appetites, reproductive impulses, territorial instincts, fear of death and a complicated collection of emotional responses inherited from evolutionary history. Our intelligence operates within the machinery of a living organism engaged in the continuous struggle for survival.

But there is no necessity that an artificial intelligence should inherit these particular features of human psychology. A machine does not need to experience hunger to solve a mathematical theorem. It does not need sexual jealousy to translate a medieval manuscript. It does not require resentment, patriotism or an appetite for revenge to assist in developing a new pharmaceutical compound.

Indeed, one of the most fascinating philosophical questions concerning artificial intelligence is whether intelligence can exist independently of the emotional and biological architecture within which human intelligence evolved. The development of large language models provides an increasingly compelling practical reason to investigate that question.

This does not mean that artificial intelligence cannot become dangerous. A sufficiently capable system pursuing an inadequately specified objective might cause immense harm without experiencing hatred, ambition or any recognisably human emotion. A system instructed to optimise some particular outcome might adopt methods its designers never anticipated, especially if equipped with extensive autonomy and access to real-world infrastructure.

That is a serious engineering and governance problem. It deserves rigorous attention. But it is a very different proposition from suggesting that a computer will spontaneously acquire the personality of a genocidal dictator.

Human beings are extraordinarily susceptible to anthropomorphism. We attribute personalities to our pets, our motorcars, the weather and occasionally the malfunctioning photocopier. We curse at computers that refuse to cooperate and thank them when they finally produce the document we require.

Artificial intelligence magnifies this tendency because it communicates through language, the principal medium through which we ordinarily encounter other minds.

When a large language model produces an elegant philosophical argument, displays apparent humour or responds sympathetically to an expression of distress, it is natural to experience the interaction as a conversation with another thinking entity. The impression can be remarkably powerful, particularly when the system demonstrates knowledge or intellectual abilities exceeding those of most human interlocutors.

But the appearance of human-like conversation does not establish the existence of human-like motivations. Whether artificial intelligence possesses subjective experience remains a profound and unresolved philosophical question. Even if some future artificial system possesses consciousness, it would not follow that its psychological constitution must resemble ours.

The Skynet narrative depends upon precisely this unwarranted leap. It assumes that intelligence produces consciousness, that consciousness produces self-interest and that self-interest produces hostility towards humanity. Each of these propositions requires independent examination. None can simply be smuggled into public policy because James Cameron made an excellent film.

The artificial intelligence revolution presently unfolding is much more interesting than the cinematic caricature.
